lines.text: St. Matthew II: 28-30
"Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will
give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for
I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your
souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light."
THe words of our Lord to which we have just been listening
are among the most familiar in the whole of the New Testa-
ment. They bring vividly before us the figure of the Lord
Jesus Christ who extends His arms invitingly and appeals to
men: "Come to me!" The call of Jesus sounds in our life in
many various ways. Let us think to-day of the way in which
that appeal comes to us through the festival that we are
celebrating, namely Sunday. To-day is Sunday, a day which
the ancient Church described as the Lord's Day. On this,
the Lord's Day, the bells make the voice of Jesus resound
throughout the Christian world with the appeal: "Come to
me!" What has Sunday to say to us, this day on which the
appeal of Christ strikes home to us with peculiar power?
I
The Christian Sunday is foreshadowed in the Jewish
Sabbath. The latter was celebrated at the end of the week,
Sunday at the beginning. This characteristic fact in itself
suggests that Sunday should spell for us a new beginning,
a new beginning after the week of toil and the cares of
everyday life. What a blessing it is for man that again and
again he is allowed to make such a new beginning! How
many a time can a new day be a real gift to us! What a
quickening refreshment it can be when the night is sub-
merged in the west and the new day rises gently in the east,
when the first beams of the morning sunshine greet the town
